title: CellDuality: Self-Supervised Reasoning in LLMs for Biology
one_liner: An LLM learns coherent biological reasoning by predicting outcomes and then checking its own predictions by working backward to the original conditions.
lead: Large language models can memorize facts about cells and drugs, but generating real biological explanations from partial information is hard because verifying whether a predicted outcome is correct usually requires a wet-lab experiment. This paper shows how an LLM can learn without ground truth by using a clever loop: predict forward (what happens to this cell when we add this drug), then predict backward (can you reconstruct which drug caused the outcome you just predicted). The fidelity of the backward reconstruction acts as a truth signal, training the model to think coherently about biology.

problem.h2: Why LLMs struggle with biological reasoning
paras: Large language models excel at recognizing patterns when you can check the answer: is this cell type annotation correct? You can look it up or count cells under a microscope. But biological reasoning is different. Suppose you ask the model to predict what happens to a human cell when you expose it to a specific drug, or to trace back from an observed cellular change to infer which genes were perturbed. There is no simple yes-or-no label, because running the experiment is expensive or impossible.

The standard fix is Reinforcement Learning from Verifiable Rewards: train the model by rewarding it when its predictions match ground-truth labels, the way you reward a chess engine when it finds the right move. But in biology, you rarely have labels for the tricky open-ended questions. You cannot easily verify a prediction, so you cannot build a reward signal.

A beginner might try: just fine-tune the model on whatever biological examples you have, then hope it works on new cases. But this breaks when the model encounters a cell type or drug combination it has never seen. The model has no internal compass pointing it toward logically consistent reasoning; it just echoes the training data.

callout.html: Most biological reasoning outcomes are non-verifiable, so you cannot use reward signals that require a human oracle to say whether the answer is right.

steps.text: LLM predicts the biological outcome (e.g., gene expression level) given initial conditions (drug, cell type).
LLM takes its own forward prediction and tries to reconstruct the original conditions.
Compare the reconstructed input to the true input; large match means the reasoning is self-consistent.
Fidelity score becomes the reward; high fidelity means the model thought coherently.
Use the fidelity reward to adjust the LLM weights via reinforcement learning, steering the model toward internally consistent reasoning.

paras: CellDuality modifies how the LLM learns by introducing a second task that the model must solve as a check on itself. Instead of training only on the forward prediction (input to outcome), the training loop now also requires the model to reverse its own prediction (outcome back to input). The model's weights are adjusted based on how well the backward reconstruction matches the real input.

hidden.h2: Reconstruction fidelity: the internal consistency score
hidden.name: Fidelity (how well reconstructed input matches real input)
paras: Fidelity is a score between 0 and 1 that measures how closely the reconstructed input resembles the true starting conditions. In practice, the paper computes this as a similarity score (e.g., a measure of how close two lists of numbers are, or exact match for discrete outcomes) between the input the model reconstructed and the actual input. High fidelity means the forward and inverse tasks are logically consistent; low fidelity means the model's predictions are internally contradictory.

The paper uses fidelity as a reward signal without ever needing a human label or a verified ground truth. Instead of asking an oracle whether the prediction is correct, it asks: did the model's own reasoning loop close consistently?

heat.caption: Darker means higher fidelity or stronger reinforcement. Highlights mark the core loop.

reads.html: Fidelity is how well you can predict backward from the model's forward answer. If the model says this drug causes a big gene response, can it then look at that gene response and correctly name the drug again? Perfect recall means perfect fidelity; confusion means the model's reasoning is incoherent.

The paper defines fidelity as the similarity between the reconstructed input and the ground-truth input, computed after both forward and inverse reasoning steps. This fidelity score serves as the intrinsic reward signal for the reinforcement learning stage, without requiring external verification labels.

paras: The core insight is that if a model's reasoning is truly coherent, it must be reversible. If you know the drug is aspirin and you predict the cell will express certain genes, and someone then shows you those gene levels, you should be able to work backward and agree it was aspirin. If your reasoning is sloppy or hallucinatory, the backward step will fail. The model cannot trick itself into high reward by cutting corners.

Here is why this creates learning pressure: when the model makes a forward prediction, it commits to an answer. The backward task immediately tests whether that commitment was logically sound. If the reconstruction is poor, the model's weights receive a small reward signal. The reinforcement learning process adjusts the weights to favor predictions that close the loop consistently. Over time, this loop trains the model to generate predictions that hang together logically, not predictions that are individually plausible but mutually contradictory.

Critically, this works without requiring a wet-lab experiment or a human label. The model bootstraps its own feedback from the structure of the problem itself. This is why CellDuality succeeds on unseen cases (drugs and cell types not in training): the model has learned to think coherently about biology, not to pattern-match training labels.

stages.s: Biological conditions: drug name, cell type
Inverse reasoning: LLM reconstructs input from outcome
Compute fidelity: how well does reconstruction match true input?
Adjust weights: reinforce predictions that close the loop
Coherent biological reasoning on unseen cases

math.words: The reward for each prediction is the fidelity score, which measures how well the reconstructed input matches the real input. The model is trained to maximize expected cumulative reward over many predictions.
symbols: the actual starting conditions (drug, cell type)
what the model guessed the input was, after working backward from its forward prediction
a score between 0 and 1, e.g., cosine distance or exact match
the reward signal used to train the model via reinforcement learning

worked.title: A tiny worked example
lines: Forward prediction: gene_X=high, gene_Y=medium (this is the model's answer).
Similarity: drug match 1.0, cell match 1.0, average = 1.0.
Reward R = 1.0 (perfect). Model weights are reinforced.
Counter-example: True input same, but model's forward was vague (gene_X=low, gene_Y=low).
Similarity: drug match 0.0, cell match 0.0, average = 0.0.
Reward R = 0.0 (failed). Model learns to avoid vague forward predictions.

math.note: The reward directly measures self-consistency: how well the model's reasoning closes the loop from input to output and back again.

bars.h2: Performance on seen vs. unseen biology

charts.title: Standard fine-tuning (baseline)
charts.note: Model memorizes training data but fails on new combinations; reasoning is brittle.

charts.title: CellDuality (this paper)
charts.note: Self-supervised loop trains coherent reasoning; model generalizes to new combinations.

items.html: If the model learns to give vague forward predictions and vague inverse predictions, the loop closes trivially but the model has not learned anything. The paper guards this by requiring the forward prediction to be specific enough that the inverse task is genuinely hard.

items.b: Mismatch between forward and inverse domains.
items.html: If the forward task predicts continuous gene levels but the inverse task reconstructs discrete drug names, the two tasks use different output spaces. The similarity score must be chosen to match the data types, or fidelity becomes uninformative.

items.b: Limited coverage on truly new cases.
items.html: The method only works if the unseen examples (drugs and cells not in training) have logically coherent explanations that can be inferred from the biological mechanisms the model saw during training. If a drug behaves in a completely new way, self-consistency alone cannot predict it.

When the forward and inverse tasks are well-aligned, fidelity becomes a true measure of reasoning coherence. The model learns to think through causality rather than pattern-match, and it generalizes correctly to new data.

demo.h2: What a runnable demo should prove
paras: Build a minimal single-cell dataset with 100 drug-cell pairs and 5 genes. Train an LLM baseline via fine-tuning, then train the same LLM with CellDuality. On a held-out test set of 50 drug-cell pairs not in training, measure: (1) how often the model correctly predicts which genes are up-regulated, (2) how well the inverse task reconstructs the original drug from the predicted gene levels, and (3) whether the model's explanations are logically consistent (e.g., does it always say the same drug causes the same phenotype).
demo.closing: The demo should show that CellDuality models maintain high fidelity even on unseen drug-cell pairs, while fine-tuning baselines guess randomly.
